subject: chemistry
title: Energy Changes Adventure 2 · Calculations
welcome_lead: Time to calculate energy changes using bond energies. We'll add, subtract and check the sign.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry bond energy calculations — ΔH from bonds broken minus bonds made.
final_note: You can now work out ΔH from bond energies and read off the sign correctly.

concepts.def: Energy to break 1 mole of a specific bond (kJ/mol)
Total energy to break all reactant bonds
Total energy released when product bonds form
Overall energy change = energy in − energy out

walkthroughs.body_html:
There are three steps every time.

1. Add up the energy to break all reactant bonds (energy in).

2. Add up the energy to make all product bonds (energy out).

3. ΔH = energy in − energy out.

If ΔH is negative, it's exothermic. If positive, endothermic.

Bonds broken: 1 × H–H (436) + 1 × Cl–Cl (243) = 679 kJ in.

Bonds made: 2 × H–Cl (432) = 864 kJ out.

ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol.

Negative, so it's exothermic — heat is released.

Common slip: forgetting the minus for exothermic. If energy out > energy in, ΔH must be negative.

Another slip: counting bonds wrong. In O₂ there's one O=O bond per molecule, not two. Always check the molecule.

And: bond energies are per mole of bonds, so multiply by how many of each bond you have.

mcqs.q: If the total energy needed to break bonds is greater than the energy released making new bonds, the reaction is...
Bond energies in tables are usually given in...

numericals.q: A reaction needs 1500 kJ to break bonds and releases 1800 kJ making new bonds. What is ΔH, in kJ/mol?
numericals.hint: ΔH = energy in − energy out. More out than in means negative.

free_texts.q: If ΔH is a positive number, is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? One word.
free_texts.hint: Positive ΔH means more energy went in than came out.
